questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a case that departs from the shared pattern is deviant
questions.stem: A release engineer compares one rollout that raised no tickets with another that raised forty. Why is the second rollout treated as a deviant case?

options.text: It departs from the pattern the other rollouts share, so it can expose what that pattern hides.
It happened on a later date, so its timeline cannot be lined up with the earlier rollouts.
options.misconception: assumes a later date alone makes a case deviant

options.text: It produced many more tickets, so a large outcome by itself marks a case as deviant.
options.misconception: believes a large outcome alone marks a case deviant

options.text: It was merged by a different engineer, so the person rather than the pattern is the outlier.
options.misconception: blames staff identity instead of the shared pattern

questions.explanation: A deviant case departs from the pattern the other cases share. A later date, a bigger ticket count or a different author may all be true of it, but none of them is what makes the case deviant.
questions.hint: Ask what the other rollouts share that this one lacks.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes two tickets a matched comparison
questions.stem: Two tickets describe a checkout failure: one from the release with the new address validator, one from the release without it. Explain what makes these two tickets a matched pair.

answer.exemplar: The two tickets are matched because the reported failure, the customer segment and the reporting period are held the same while the presence of the new address validator is the only systematic difference between them. Holding the other conditions constant is what lets the pair speak to the validator rather than to anything else that changed nearby.

questions.explanation: Matching holds the conditions that could produce the outcome constant while one condition varies. Here the failure and the customer type match while the validator differs, so the pair speaks to the validator.
questions.hint: Name the condition that is held constant across the pair.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a proposed pair fails to isolate its condition of interest

stimulus.body: A sprint retrospective lists four failed releases. Two came from a small team working on a single service; the other two came from a large team rewriting the deployment pipeline across a whole platform. A researcher wants to compare the two groups and proposes pairing one small-team release with one large-team release.

questions.stem: Given that thread, what is the strongest objection to the proposed pairing of one small-team release with one large-team release?

options.text: The pair differs on team size, tooling, service count and cadence at once, so nothing can be credited.
options.misconception: objects to sample size, not to what differs between the cases

options.text: The large-team release may share little with the small-team one, so a shared outcome shows no shared cause.
A comparison needs more than two cases on each side before it counts, so two and two is too thin.
options.misconception: believes a comparison needs more than two cases on each side

options.text: Drop the small-team releases and describe only the large-team pattern, since small teams are unusual.
options.misconception: wants the small-team cases removed because they are unusual

questions.explanation: The proposed pair differs on many conditions at once, so a shared outcome cannot be tied to one condition. A pair that differs on little beside the condition of interest is what can support a claim.
questions.hint: Check how many conditions change between the two releases.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: State what a chosen pair supports and where the claim stops
questions.stem: A team paired two releases that differed only in a new caching layer and claims the layer caused the drop in page latency. What can this pair properly be claimed to show?

options.text: That the caching layer will cut latency for every future release of the product.
options.misconception: extends the pair's finding to untested future releases

options.text: That no release without the layer can ever be as fast as these two releases were.
options.misconception: turns the pair's result into a claim of impossibility elsewhere

options.text: That the layer lowered latency in the two releases that were compared, and nothing beyond that pair.
That the team has identified the single most effective way to speed up the product overall.
options.misconception: treats one controlled pair as a full ranking of all causes

questions.explanation: A matched pair supports a claim about the cases it contains: the condition differed and the outcome differed with it. It says nothing about untested releases, other causes, or what is possible elsewhere.
questions.hint: State the boundary of what the compared releases cover.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analysing inside one case and across two
questions.learningObjective: Plan an analysis that uses two cases without overreaching
questions.stem: A support lead wants to know whether a slow search feature causes abandoned carts. She has one detailed ticket from a user who abandoned a cart during search, and a second from a user who completed checkout without touching search. How should she use these two tickets?

options.text: Call the abandoning shopper typical and the completing one deviant, then report a broad finding.
options.misconception: treats one abandoning shopper as typical of all shoppers

options.text: Generalise from the two detailed tickets to all shoppers who used search that week, because detail implies coverage.
options.misconception: believes two detailed cases can settle a rate for all shoppers

options.text: Use the two tickets to count how often search delays appear in the logs, and report that count as the effect size.
options.misconception: confuses a log count of delay mentions with the effect on carts

options.text: Contrast the two tickets on whether the delay occurred, then check what else differed before concluding.

questions.explanation: Two detailed tickets support a contrast on the condition of interest only if the cases are otherwise comparable, which is checked first. A pair cannot give a rate, and one case cannot stand for all shoppers.
questions.hint: Separate what a pair can show from what a count would show.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: State what evidence each step of a traced sequence requires
questions.stem: A ticket thread describes a deploy, then a spike in errors, then a rollback. What must a tracing of that chain establish at each step?

options.text: The evidence that each step of the chain actually occurred, not merely that the steps were listed in order.
That the rollback fixed the problem, so the deploy must have caused the errors it followed.
options.misconception: treats the rollback as proof the deploy caused the errors

options.text: That the errors began within one minute of the deploy, since a tight gap always indicates causation.
options.misconception: believes a short time gap alone establishes causation

options.text: That the deploy was the only change in the release, so no other change need be considered.
options.misconception: assumes a single change means other changes cannot matter

questions.explanation: A traced chain is only as strong as the evidence for each link, and a list of steps is not evidence they happened. A rollback shows a symptom stopped, not that an earlier step caused it.
questions.hint: Ask what record shows each arrow in the chain.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unobserved step inside a traced chain
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an unobserved step weakens a traced chain
questions.stem: A traced chain in a ticket thread runs from a config change to a restart to a rise in failed jobs. The restart itself was never logged. Explain what this gap does to the chain.

answer.exemplar: The unlogged restart is an unobserved step, so the chain has a missing link: the order of the two recorded events is known, but nothing in the thread shows that the restart fell between them or that anything happened during it. The chain can therefore describe a sequence of events that happened, but it cannot claim that the config change and the failed jobs were connected through the restart, because that middle step is asserted rather than evidenced.

questions.explanation: An unobserved step breaks the evidence between the events on either side. The recorded order still holds, but the link from the config change to the failed jobs rests on an inference nothing documents.
questions.hint: Note what the thread never records about the middle.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rival explanation and the test that separates them
questions.learningObjective: Select a test that separates two rival explanations

stimulus.body: A ticket records that after a change to the retry library, failed payments began to be reported as successful. A second note in the same ticket says a vendor outage happened the same morning. A third note says the outage was traced to a certificate error in the vendor's own network.

questions.stem: Given this thread, which test would best separate the retry change from the vendor outage as the cause of the reported successes?

options.text: Re-running the failed payments from before the retry change on the same connection to see if they still report success.
options.misconception: replays the same cases instead of separating the two conditions

options.text: Checking payments that went through the vendor outage but skipped the retry change, and payments that hit the retry change while the vendor was healthy.
Comparing the number of support complaints before and after the retry change, since complaint volume tracks real defects.
options.misconception: treats complaint counts as a direct measure of the cause

options.text: Asking the team that wrote the retry change to confirm whether they believe the change was safe to ship.
options.misconception: asks for an opinion instead of a test that separates causes

questions.explanation: Separating rival causes means finding cases that differ on one cause while the other is held fixed. Payments through the outage without the retry change, and payments with the change during healthy hours, do that.
questions.hint: Look for cases where only one of the two causes is present.

options.misconception: picks the unusual case because it looks more dramatic

options.text: Neither ticket, because typicality is decided by the number of complaints rather than by the shared pattern.
options.misconception: judges typicality by complaint count instead of a shared pattern

options.text: Ticket 118, because it matches the pattern held across the other billing tickets, while 119 departs from it.
Both tickets, because a typical case is one that highlights the most complex path through the system.
options.misconception: believes a typical case is the one with the most complex path

questions.explanation: A typical case is one that shares the pattern found across the cases in the study, which is what makes it a fair representative. Ticket 119 is the deviant here because its override and late payment depart from that pattern.
questions.hint: Ask which ticket shares what the other billing tickets share.

options.text: The two releases may differ on many conditions at once, so a difference in queue growth cannot be credited to any single one.
One release produced a bigger queue, so it should be paired with the release that produced no tickets at all.
options.misconception: pairs on the size of the outcome instead of the condition

options.text: Two releases cannot show a contrast, because a contrast needs at least ten releases on each side of the split.
options.misconception: demands a fixed large number of releases before any contrast

options.text: The pair should be dropped entirely, since release-level comparisons never support any conclusion at all.
options.misconception: believes release comparisons can never support a conclusion

questions.explanation: A pair that differs on many conditions at once cannot attribute an outcome difference to any single condition. Choosing one release that grew the queue and one that did not says nothing about what the two share.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: Set the boundary of a claim drawn from a single pair
questions.stem: A pair of tickets compares a release with a new retry policy against a release without it, and both show the same rise in failed logins. Explain what that pair can and cannot be claimed to show.

answer.exemplar: The pair shows that in the two releases compared, the rise in failed logins occurred while the retry policy was present in one and absent in the other, and it shows the two cases could be matched on the features the researcher held constant. It cannot show that the retry policy causes the rise in general, that releases without the policy are safe, or that the policy is the main driver, because one pair of releases carries no information about untested cases or about competing explanations.

questions.explanation: The pair carries a claim about the two releases it contains and nothing outside them. It cannot extend to untested releases, rule out competing causes, or rank causes, because one pair says nothing about those.
questions.hint: Mark where the evidence of the pair stops.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analysing inside one case and across two
questions.learningObjective: Choose an analysis that keeps single-case and paired claims apart

stimulus.body: A ticket records a customer who enabled two-factor sign-in, was locked out for an hour, and then unlocked the account after a support agent intervened. A second ticket records another customer who enabled the same setting and was never locked out, with no agent involved.

questions.stem: Given these two tickets, what is the most defensible way to use them in an analysis?

options.text: Treat the second ticket as the typical case and the first as the deviant one, and report the pair as showing most users are unaffected.
options.misconception: labels one ticket typical and reads the pair as a general result

options.text: Analyse each ticket on its own for what the lockout and the agent intervention show, and treat the two together as a contrast whose limits are stated.
Combine the two tickets into a single count of how often two-factor sign-in leads to a lockout and report that rate.
options.misconception: turns two case accounts into a rate neither ticket supports

options.text: Discard the first ticket because its agent intervention makes it unlike ordinary use of the setting.
options.misconception: discards a case because it contains an unusual element

questions.explanation: One case supports a claim about what happened inside it; a pair supports a contrast only when the cases are comparable. A rate needs many accounts, and odd elements often make a case informative.
questions.hint: Ask what each account can show on its own and together.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: Judge how far a traced sequence supports a claim about cause
questions.stem: A traced sequence in a ticket runs: disk fills, writes slow, cache evictions rise, requests time out. Which statement about this chain is best supported?

options.text: The disk filling caused the timeouts, since each link in the chain follows from the one before it.
options.misconception: takes a plausible ordering as proof the first step caused the last

options.text: The chain proves that filling the disk is the only possible source of the timeouts in the system.
options.misconception: claims uniqueness of the cause from a single observed chain

options.text: The links are consistent with one another in the recorded order, and the timeout followed the evictions in the logs.
The timeout caused the disk to fill, because the chain shows a sequence of events rather than a direction of cause.
options.misconception: reverses the causal direction because a chain only shows ordering

questions.explanation: The chain supports a statement about order: the links sit in that order in the records and the timeouts came after the evictions. It does not settle which link produced the next, nor does it prove a unique cause.
questions.hint: Distinguish a supported ordering from a supported cause.

questions.stem: A traced chain in a support thread runs from a routine upgrade to a jump in memory use to slow page loads. No log records anything between the upgrade and the jump. What should the analyst do first?

options.text: Assume the upgrade caused the jump, since the jump is the first measurement taken after the upgrade.
options.misconception: fills the evidence gap with the most convenient assumption

options.text: Drop the middle of the chain and report only that slow page loads followed the upgrade in the thread.
options.misconception: drops the weak step and reports the rest as if it were sound

options.text: Report the whole chain as established, because each of the three steps is named in the thread.
options.misconception: treats naming a step as if it were evidencing that step

options.text: Mark the middle step as unobserved and look for the record that would have shown it before relying on the chain.

questions.explanation: An unobserved step is a gap, and the two ends cannot close it. The analyst should look for the record that would have shown the step and, failing that, mark the chain as broken there.
questions.hint: Ask what record would have documented the missing step.

Confirm that the bug is real and reproducible, since until that is settled the explanations cannot be weighed.
options.misconception: confuses proving the bug exists with separating the explanations

options.misconception: ranks causes by how common they are rather than by evidence

options.misconception: treats the reporter's guess as better evidence than a test

questions.explanation: Two explanations are separated by evidence that would differ under each, not by confirming the failure is real. Commonness and opinion are weak stand-ins for a case present under one explanation and absent under the other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a deviant case is kept in a comparison
questions.stem: A support manager has one ticket where a form rejected a valid postcode and one where a form accepted a postcode that should fail. Explain how the manager should treat these two cases.

answer.exemplar: The manager should treat the rejecting ticket as a deviant case and the accepting ticket as typical, because the accepting ticket shows the behaviour that the rest of the tickets in the batch also show while the rejecting one departs from it. The deviant case is worth keeping precisely because it forces the account to add something the typical case alone does not show, and its departure should be described in terms of the shared pattern rather than as an isolated defect.

questions.explanation: A deviant case is identified by the pattern the typical cases share, and it is kept because it is where the account is tested. Calling the rejecting ticket deviant means asking what the pattern must add to explain it.
questions.hint: Say which case departs from the batch's shared pattern.

questions.stem: A support thread traces a sequence: traffic doubles, queue depth grows, response time doubles, users begin to time out. Explain what this sequence establishes and what it does not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Assign typical and deviant roles from the pattern in the set
questions.stem: A team has a ticket with a normal search response and a ticket with a search that returned nothing. Which pair of roles should these two cases play in a comparison?

options.text: Both should be typical cases, because they show two different parts of the search feature working.
options.misconception: calls both cases typical because they cover different code paths

options.text: The normal response should be deviant, since a working feature is the surprising outcome in a bug report set.
options.misconception: treats the working case as the surprising one in a bug collection

options.text: The empty result should be deviant and the normal response typical, with no further check of the pattern.
options.misconception: assigns the roles without checking what the pattern actually is

options.text: One case should be checked against the shared pattern to learn which is typical, and the other treated as the deviant case.

questions.explanation: The roles depend on the pattern running through the set, so the team must establish that pattern before labelling either ticket. The matching case is typical and the other is deviant.
questions.hint: Establish the shared pattern before assigning the roles.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: State the claim a well matched pair supports
questions.stem: A researcher matches two tickets on customer segment, subscription tier and week of contact, and differs only on whether a caching change was live. What does this pair support?

options.text: A claim about the caching change within the matched conditions, and about nothing outside them.
A claim about caching across all customers, since the conditions were matched so carefully.
options.misconception: extends a matched finding to customers the match never covered

options.text: No claim at all, because matching on so many features leaves no room for a difference to be informative.
options.misconception: thinks a thorough match leaves no room for a real difference

options.text: A claim about the caching change plus a claim about any later change the team might consider.
options.misconception: adds claims about untried changes to the one the pair supports

questions.explanation: Matching on segment, tier and week while varying only the caching change is what makes the contrast informative. The result is a claim about that change in those conditions, not a claim about other customers.
questions.hint: Say which condition varied and which stayed fixed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: Explain the weakness of a pair with many moving conditions
questions.stem: A team pairs a ticket from a quiet Tuesday with a ticket from the busiest hour of launch week. Explain what problems this pairing raises for the claim the team wants to make.

answer.exemplar: The pairing varies the conditions that are most likely to matter: the level of load on the system and the time of day on which the tickets were filed. Because several conditions move together with the outcome, any difference in the reported failures could be produced by load, by the hour, or by the change under investigation, and the pair provides no way to tell which. A usable pair would need the load and timing held steady across both cases, leaving only the condition of interest free to vary, and the current pairing cannot support a causal claim of that kind.

questions.explanation: The pairing lets load, timing and the change under study vary together, so a difference in failures cannot be credited to any of them. A workable pair would hold load and timing steady and let only the condition of interest vary.
questions.hint: Ask how many conditions moved with the outcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: Set the limits of a claim drawn from a matched pair

stimulus.body: A ticket reports that a scheduled report arrived three hours late. A second ticket from the same week reports the same report arriving on time. The two tickets share the same account, the same report and the same week, and differ in whether the nightly job was moved to a different machine that week.

questions.stem: Given this thread, what is the most accurate statement about what these two tickets show?

options.text: They show that moving the job to another machine makes reports late, for every account that does the same.
options.misconception: generalises a single week to every account that runs the same job

options.text: They show that in this account and week the lateness accompanied the move to another machine, and no more than that.
They show that the report is unreliable in general, because the two tickets disagree about the same week.
options.misconception: reads a disagreement between two cases as a defect in the service

options.text: They show that the move to another machine is the one cause of lateness, since the two tickets differ on that point.
options.misconception: treats one varied condition as the single cause of the outcome

questions.explanation: The pair varies the machine and holds the account, report and week steady, so it supports a bounded observation about this account this week. It cannot travel to other accounts or settle which cause produced the lateness.
questions.hint: Mark the boundary of the account and week in the ticket.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analysing inside one case and across two
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two evidence types support together
questions.stem: A team holds one full ticket narrative and a table of forty short failure descriptions. What can the two together support better than either alone?

options.text: They can support a precise causal claim, because the table supplies the sample the narrative lacks.
options.misconception: believes a table of cases supplies the missing mechanism

options.text: They can support nothing, because a detailed narrative and a table cannot be used in one study.
options.misconception: insists the two kinds of evidence cannot appear in one study

options.text: They can support a claim about the pattern in the table and a close account of the mechanism in the narrative.
They can support a rate that neither source supports, since combining them multiplies their reach.
options.misconception: thinks combining sources multiplies what each source can support

questions.explanation: The table shows the pattern and its extent, while the narrative shows the mechanism inside one case, and each carries what the other cannot. Neither source reaches a rate, and combining them does not create one.
questions.hint: Ask what each source carries that the other lacks.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: Decide what must be established before reading a trace as a cause
questions.stem: A thread traces: a retry limit is lowered, requests start failing at 1 a.m., latency alerts fire. What should the team establish before treating this as a cause?

options.text: That the retry limit was lowered deliberately, since an accidental change carries no responsibility.
options.misconception: treats intent as the missing support for a causal reading

options.text: That the alerts fired close to 1 a.m., since a narrow gap strengthens the sequence.
options.misconception: leans on time proximity in place of evidence for each link

options.text: That requests failed before the limit changed, since failures that came first would change the order.
options.misconception: insists failures must precede the change for the order to hold

options.text: What record supports each step, and what else could account for a 1 a.m. rise in failures.

questions.explanation: A trace earns the word cause only when each step has its own record, and a 1 a.m. failure spike has routine causes such as a nightly job. The team must check records and routine explanations first.
questions.hint: Look for routine explanations of the early-morning spike.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unobserved step inside a traced chain
questions.learningObjective: Describe the status of a chain with an unobserved link
questions.stem: A traced chain of four steps rests on a middle step that no record shows happened. What is the correct description of the chain's status?

options.text: The chain has an unobserved link, so the claims that cross that link are weaker than the claims within either side.
The chain is broken and therefore empty, since no part of it can be used once one link is missing.
options.misconception: treats one missing link as voiding the evidence on both sides of it

options.text: The chain is complete, since the surrounding records fix the middle step between them by elimination.
options.misconception: believes surrounding records fix the missing step by elimination

options.text: The chain is stronger than usual, since the unobserved step is the one place a rival account can be tested.
options.misconception: mistakes a weakness in the chain for a strength of the design

questions.explanation: An unobserved link leaves a gap the surrounding records cannot close, so claims crossing it carry less weight than claims inside one side. The chain stays usable in parts, and the gap marks where to test a rival account.
questions.hint: Say which claims cross the gap and which do not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rival explanation and the test that separates them
questions.learningObjective: Specify the content of a test that separates rival explanations
questions.stem: A checkout failure has two candidate explanations: a bank-side decline and a bug in the retry logic. Explain what a test that separates them would have to contain.

answer.exemplar: A separating test must contain cases in which one of the two candidate causes is present and the other is absent, with the remaining conditions held the same. Retrying a decline that the bank really did issue, against a decline the bank never issued because the retry logic sent the request twice, would give different results under each explanation and so would tell the team which account fits. A test that only reproduces the failure tells the team that the failure is real, and that is compatible with both explanations at once.

questions.explanation: A separating test needs cases where one explanation is present and the other absent, with the rest held the same. Reproducing the failure shows only that it is real, and that fits both explanations.
questions.hint: Ask what each explanation would predict for the result.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Use deviant cases as tests of the shared pattern

stimulus.body: A team collects twenty-eight tickets about a search box. Twenty-six describe a search that returned results, with wording, filters and response times in a narrow range. Two describe a search that returned nothing: one names a rare product code, the other names a product code the system was told to exclude.

questions.stem: Given this thread, how should the two empty-result tickets be used?

options.text: As two typical cases, because they cover the edge of the search behaviour that the other tickets miss.
options.misconception: labels edge cases typical because they cover behaviour others miss

options.text: As deviant cases, because each departs from the pattern the other twenty-six tickets share.
As cases to be dropped, because tickets that deviate from the pattern distort the results of the study.
options.misconception: removes deviating cases from the study instead of explaining them

options.text: As a basis for a new claim about excluded codes, since the pair shows a shared cause for empty results.
options.misconception: reads the pair as establishing a shared cause for the empty results

questions.explanation: Both empty-result tickets depart from the pattern the other twenty-six share, so they are deviant rather than typical. They are kept because they test the account, and each needs its own explanation.
questions.hint: Compare the two tickets against the pattern in the rest.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: Formulate the strongest claim a matched pair can carry
questions.stem: Two tickets match on account type, plan, weekday and hour, and differ on whether a new export library was live. The matched pair shows slower exports in the live case. What is the strongest claim available?

options.text: The new export library slows exports for every account, because the match was careful and the difference was clear.
options.misconception: extends the matched result to every account regardless of conditions

options.text: The two tickets disagree about export speed, so the difference is measurement noise rather than a real effect.
options.misconception: dismisses a consistent difference between matched cases as noise

options.text: In these matched accounts and conditions, the slower export occurred with the new library live.
The new export library is the most effective export approach, because the pair shows a clear difference.
options.misconception: ranks approaches on the strength of a single controlled pair

questions.explanation: The match makes the difference meaningful, so the claim can say the slower export came with the library in the conditions matched. It cannot reach untested accounts or rank approaches, since one pair does neither.
questions.hint: State the claim inside the boundary of the match.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: Prepare a pair by controlling the condition of interest
questions.stem: A ticket records a slow report on a workstation with a spinning disk and another records a fast report on a machine with a solid-state disk. What should the analyst do before pairing them?

options.text: Pair them directly, because the storage type is the condition of interest and the reports ran the same way.
options.misconception: pairs cases whose other conditions were never compared

options.text: Add a third case with a slow disk, so the two machine types are each represented twice.
options.misconception: adds cases on the strength of symmetry rather than of fit

options.text: Drop the disk detail from both tickets, since hardware differences are noise once a report is slow.
options.misconception: strips the detail that defines the condition of interest

options.text: Check what else the two cases share, then hold steady or vary the disk type deliberately rather than by accident.

questions.explanation: Pairing needs cases alike except on the condition of interest, and two tickets from different people are rarely that alike. The analyst must check what else they share and control the disk type.
questions.hint: Check what the two cases share besides the disk type.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: Judge the standing of a claim by the comparison behind it
questions.stem: A claim says the new queue library caused the backlog to grow in a two-release comparison. Which statement best describes the claim's standing?

options.text: It is a claim about what happened in the two releases compared, and it has not been carried beyond them.
It is a claim about the library in general, because a controlled comparison licenses general conclusions.
options.misconception: believes a controlled comparison licenses general conclusions

options.text: It is a claim with no standing at all, since a claim always needs more than two releases behind it.
options.misconception: insists no claim is possible without a large number of releases

options.text: It is a claim about the team that chose the library, since causes are attributed to whoever made the choice.
options.misconception: redirects a causal claim towards the people who made the choice

questions.explanation: A claim is only as broad as the comparison behind it, and a two-release comparison speaks to those two releases. Control makes the difference meaningful; it does not widen the range the claim covers.
questions.hint: Ask how far the comparison actually reaches.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analysing inside one case and across two
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish mechanistic and pattern claims across evidence types
questions.stem: A team has one ticket for a user whose search returned a wrong price, and a table of sixty searches with the prices they returned. Explain what the ticket and the table each support.

answer.exemplar: The single ticket supports a close account of one mechanism: it can show how the wrong price was produced in that session, what the user saw and what the system logged, because the record is detailed enough to reconstruct the path. The table supports a different kind of statement: across sixty searches it can show how often wrong prices appeared and in which circumstances, which is a pattern claim rather than a mechanistic one. Neither source reaches a rate on its own, and the table cannot explain the mechanism that the ticket documents.

questions.explanation: The ticket supports a close account of one mechanism because it records the path in detail. The table supports a claim about how often the problem appeared across many searches, but not how it happened.
questions.hint: Ask what each source can and cannot reach.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a traced sequence against a rival account in the record

stimulus.body: A thread records: a certificate is rotated on Tuesday, on Thursday a partner starts rejecting requests, on Friday the partner's own status page mentions a certificate error of their own. A comment in the thread notes the rotation was applied correctly and the request format did not change.

questions.stem: Given this thread, which description of the traced sequence is best supported?

options.text: The certificate rotation caused the rejection, because it happened first in the timeline.
options.misconception: treats the earliest event in a timeline as the cause of the rest

options.text: The partner's own certificate error is a live rival explanation, and the rotation's role is not established by the thread.
The rotation is cleared of blame, because a correct rotation cannot contribute to a rejection.
options.misconception: clears a cause because its own step was performed correctly

options.text: The thread proves the request format changed, because the rejection followed the rotation by two days.
options.misconception: claims the format changed on no evidence in the thread

questions.explanation: The thread records a correct rotation and a partner-side error on the same day, so the rotation's role is unestablished rather than excluded. A timeline starting with the rotation does not make it the cause.
questions.hint: Check for a competing cause recorded at the same time.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unobserved step inside a traced chain
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a drawn step against a recorded one in a chain
questions.stem: A traced chain of three steps has a middle step that appears only in a diagram drawn by the author, with no record behind it. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: The chain is complete, because a diagram in the ticket is itself a record of what happened.
options.misconception: treats a drawn diagram as a record equivalent to a log

options.text: The chain cannot be used at all, so the two recorded steps should be reported as two unrelated events.
options.misconception: voids the recorded steps along with the inferred one

options.text: The chain stands on its two recorded ends, and the middle link remains an inference the author supplied.
The chain is strengthened, because a diagram shows the author thought the steps through in order.
options.misconception: reads careful diagramming as independent evidence of the step

questions.explanation: A diagram records what the author believed, not what the system did, so the middle link stays an inference. The two recorded steps keep their value, and the diagram is a hypothesis needing evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the diagram records anything that happened.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rival explanation and the test that separates them
questions.learningObjective: Plan the first test for a fault with two candidate causes
questions.stem: A flaky upload fails roughly one time in twenty, and the team suspects either disk pressure or a race in the uploader. What should the team build first?

options.text: A test that runs the upload a thousand times and counts the failures, so the team knows how common the problem is.
options.misconception: measures how often the failure occurs instead of what causes it

options.text: A test that raises disk pressure and records whether failures cluster, so one explanation is stressed directly.
options.misconception: stresses one explanation without a comparison against the other

options.text: A test that removes the uploader's locking and records the failure rate, so the code path is simplified.
options.misconception: changes the code under test, which invalidates the comparison

options.text: A test with conditions where one cause is present and the other absent, and a clear signal that tells the two apart.

questions.explanation: A flaky fault needs conditions that separate the explanations, plus a signal that points one way under one cause and the other way under the rival. Counting failures gives frequency, not cause.
questions.hint: Look for conditions that isolate one cause from the other.

questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Identify a deviant case from the pattern across a batch
questions.stem: One ticket in a batch describes a chart that rendered blank; the other twenty-seven describe charts that rendered correctly. What does this make the blank-chart ticket?

options.text: The deviant case for the batch, since it departs from the pattern the other tickets share.
A typical case, since blank output is the outcome the batch was collected to study.
options.misconception: confuses relevance to the study question with typicality

options.text: A case with no role, because only cases that fit the pattern can be used at all.
options.misconception: believes cases outside the pattern have no place in the study

options.text: A second deviant case, since a rendering failure is always unusual by definition.
options.misconception: counts the case twice by calling it a second deviant case

questions.explanation: Deviance is judged by the pattern the rest of the batch shares, and only one ticket departs from it. Relevance to the question is separate, and a rendering failure is not deviant by definition.
questions.hint: Judge the ticket against the pattern in the other tickets.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: Rebuild a pair so that one condition varies and the rest hold
questions.stem: Two tickets describe a failed payment at checkout: one from a customer using a prepaid card, one from a customer using a credit card on a savings account. Explain how a researcher should build a pair from them.

answer.exemplar: The researcher cannot use these two tickets as they stand, because they differ on the payment instrument and on the account type at the same time, and each of those differences could produce the failure. A workable pair would be one from a prepaid card and one from a credit card, with the account type, the amount, the time of day and the merchant held the same, so that the payment instrument is the only condition free to vary. Only a pair built that way can support a claim about the instrument itself rather than about a bundle of differences.

questions.explanation: The two tickets differ on two conditions at once, so the pair cannot support a claim about either. A workable pair would vary the payment instrument while holding account type, amount, time and merchant steady.
questions.hint: List the conditions that move together in the two tickets.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: Identify uncontrolled variation in a proposed pair

stimulus.body: A researcher selects one ticket filed in January by a customer on a trial plan and one filed in July by a customer on a paid plan. The two tickets report the same feature failing, but the January customer is on a region that was migrated in March, and the July customer is not.

questions.stem: Given this thread, which objection to this pairing is strongest?

options.text: The pair should keep the January customer, because the earliest tickets are usually the most reliable ones.
options.misconception: prefers early reports on the grounds that they are older and neater

options.text: The two cases differ in plan, season and migration region together, so no single condition in the pair can be credited with the failure.
The pair should use two customers on the same plan, because matching on plan alone makes the comparison decisive.
options.misconception: believes matching on one condition is enough to make a pair decisive

options.text: The pair is acceptable, because the identical symptom means the relevant conditions have been controlled.
options.misconception: treats a shared symptom as evidence that the conditions were controlled

questions.explanation: Plan, season and migration region all vary, so the shared symptom cannot be credited to any of them. Holding plan steady alone leaves the same problem, since the other varying conditions stay free.
questions.hint: Count the conditions that differ between the two cases.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a supported statement from an overreaching one
questions.stem: A team ran two matched tickets and saw a clear difference in the outcome. What must the team still avoid claiming?

options.text: That the tickets in the pair shared the features the researcher held constant.
options.misconception: denies a feature of the pair that the comparison record supports

options.text: That the outcome differed between the two cases that were compared.
options.misconception: denies a difference the comparison actually recorded

options.text: That the finding extends to releases, accounts and periods that were not compared.
That the pair was built so the condition of interest was the only thing free to vary.
options.misconception: denies a design feature that made the comparison meaningful

questions.topic: Analysing inside one case and across two
questions.learningObjective: Combine a detailed case with a list without blurring their claims
questions.stem: A team has one long ticket from a customer whose invoice was wrong and a short list of nine other wrong invoices. What is the best way to use both together?

options.text: Read the long ticket closely, and quote the list to show that the problem is common across customers.
options.misconception: uses a short list as though it carried a proper frequency

options.text: Read the long ticket for the mechanism, and use the list to say how widely the problem appears.
Add the nine to the long ticket and treat the result as a single case study of ten failures.
options.misconception: merges a detailed case and a list into one unit of analysis

options.text: Read the long ticket for the mechanism, and treat the nine as a pattern sample with its own limits.
options.misconception: reads the short list as if it carried a frequency with a denominator

questions.explanation: The long ticket carries the mechanism for one session and the list the pattern across customers, so they serve different purposes. Neither yields a rate alone, and merging them blurs the source of claims.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: State what a multi-system traced sequence establishes
questions.stem: A traced sequence shows a service, a setting change, and a slower response, with each step recorded in a different system. What does this sequence establish?

options.text: That the three events occurred in that order, as the separate records show, and it is silent on what linked them.
That the setting change caused the slower response, because the three records line up in sequence.
options.misconception: treats a consistent ordering as proof of the mechanism

options.text: That the service was responsible for the change, since the service appears first in the list of steps.
options.misconception: assigns blame to the first element listed in a sequence

options.text: That the records were all produced by the same system, since one thread collects all three of them.
options.misconception: assumes one collection point means one originating system

questions.explanation: Records in three separate systems establish that the events happened in that order and no more. A recorded order is not yet a mechanism, because a mechanism needs evidence that the steps are linked.
questions.hint: Ask what the separate records show about links.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unobserved step inside a traced chain
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limit of a chain with an unrecorded deploy
questions.stem: A traced chain links a code change to a rise in errors, but the deploy that carried the change into production is not recorded anywhere. Explain what the chain can and cannot claim.

answer.exemplar: Without a record of the deploy, the chain asserts that the change reached production without showing it, so the step between the code change and the rise in errors rests on an assumption rather than evidence. The chain can therefore claim that the change was written before the errors rose and that a deploy is the usual way such a change becomes live. It cannot claim that this change was the one running when the errors began, because the thread contains nothing that ties the two together, and the gap marks the exact point at which a different explanation could still fit.

questions.explanation: The chain asserts that the change reached production without showing it, so the link to the errors rests on an assumption. It can claim the order of recorded events, but not that this change was running when errors began.
questions.hint: Say which link the missing record would have closed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rival explanation and the test that separates them
questions.learningObjective: Select the comparison that isolates each of two causes

stimulus.body: A ticket reports a 12% drop in successful checkouts after a pricing page change. A comment says a payment provider had a 30-minute incident the same afternoon. questions.stem: Given this thread, which test would most cleanly separate the pricing change from the provider incident?

options.text: Compare checkout success before and after the pricing change across all payment methods, since the change affected all of them.
options.misconception: uses the change as the only difference and ignores the provider window

options.text: Compare non-card checkouts across the change with card checkouts outside the incident window, so each cause is present alone.
Replay the provider's status page for the afternoon and check whether the outage is listed as the main cause.
options.misconception: reads a public status page as though it settled the question

options.text: Count the support tickets raised about checkouts in the three days around the change, since volume tracks the effect.
options.misconception: counts complaints as a proxy for the outcome being explained

questions.explanation: The causes can be separated because the incident touched only card payments while the change touched every method. Comparing non-card checkouts across the change with card checkouts outside the incident isolates them.
questions.hint: Use the difference in what each cause affected.

questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Assign roles and state the obligation a deviant case creates
questions.stem: A batch of tickets is gathered about login failures. Most record a wrong password; one records a valid password rejected after a password reset. What role should each play?

options.text: Both are typical, because login failures of any kind belong in the same study of the login feature.
options.misconception: pools cases that depart from the pattern into one typical group

options.text: The wrong-password ticket is deviant, because the unusual one is easier to explain.
options.misconception: treats the easier case as the deviant one for convenience

options.text: The wrong-password ticket is typical and the reset ticket is deviant, so the account must add something for the reset case.
Both are deviant, because a batch is defined by the cases that depart from the ordinary pattern.
options.misconception: believes a batch is made of the cases that break the pattern

questions.explanation: Typicality follows the pattern most tickets share, which here is the wrong-password case. The reset ticket departs from it, so the account must add something for it, which is where the explanation gets tested.
questions.hint: Let the majority pattern decide which case is typical.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: Publish a matched result without widening its scope
questions.stem: Two tickets match on browser, account plan, page and time of day, and differ on whether a cache was cleared that morning. The result shows the cached case loading faster. What should the team do with that result?

options.text: Publish it as a finding about the product's speed, since the match was thorough.
options.misconception: treats a careful match as a licence for a product-wide claim

options.text: Publish it as a finding about the cache, since the cache was the only condition that varied.
options.misconception: overstates a pair as a general finding about the cache

options.text: Run the pair again, because a single pair can never support a claim of any kind.
options.misconception: insists a single pair can never support any claim at all

options.text: State the claim for the matched conditions, and say that the team has not yet tested the cache elsewhere.

questions.explanation: The pair supports a claim about cache clearing in the conditions it matched, and the team should say so plainly. Publishing it as a finding about the product would carry the claim past the compared cases.
questions.hint: Write the claim inside the conditions that were matched.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose bundled conditions in a proposed pair
questions.stem: A pairing proposal sets one ticket from a small team beside one from a large team, both reporting the same slow build. What is the main defect in the proposal?

options.text: Many conditions travel together with the outcome, so the pair cannot attribute the slow build to any of them.
The two teams report the same symptom, so the pair is too similar to show a contrast at all.
options.misconception: believes a contrast requires the two symptoms to differ

options.text: Team size cannot be observed reliably enough to serve as a condition in a comparison.
options.misconception: dismisses a condition because it is hard to measure precisely

options.text: A build that is slow is not a suitable outcome, since only failures belong in a study.
options.misconception: restricts outcomes to failures and rules out slow successes

questions.explanation: Team size is bundled with tooling, process and repository size, so the shared outcome cannot be credited to any of them. A contrast needs cases that differ in the symptom and are alike in what could explain it.
questions.hint: Check what else travels with the team size difference.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: Phrase a claim so that it matches the comparison behind it
questions.stem: A team claims that two matched tickets show the new check was the reason a payment failed. Explain how the team should phrase the claim and why.

answer.exemplar: The team should phrase the claim as holding for the two tickets it compared: in those cases, the payment failed with the new check in place and succeeded without it, under the conditions the researcher held constant. The reason is that a matched pair licenses a claim about the cases it contains and nothing beyond them, so wording that says the new check was the reason in general would be a claim about untested cases that the design never examined. Naming the boundary is not a weakness in the finding; it is what makes the finding usable.

questions.explanation: The claim should name the two compared tickets and the conditions held constant, because a matched pair licenses a claim about the cases it contains. General wording would extend it to cases never examined.
questions.hint: Name the cases and the conditions inside the claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analysing inside one case and across two
questions.learningObjective: Run an analysis that keeps the mechanism and the contrast apart

stimulus.body: A ticket records a customer who could not complete a checkout after the postcode field was changed on the delivery page. A second ticket records a customer who completed a checkout after the same change, using an address in a region the form had always accepted. A third note says the postcode validation was tested on the old format only.

questions.stem: Given these tickets, what is the most defensible analysis to run?

options.text: Treat the failing customer as the deviant case and the succeeding one as typical, and report the pair as showing the change is safe.
options.misconception: labels the pair safe because one customer succeeded after the change

options.text: Analyse the failing ticket closely for the mechanism, and use the succeeding ticket to show the outcome depends on the address format.
Count how often checkouts fail after the change, since the two tickets suggest a general failure rate.
options.misconception: turns two case accounts into a failure rate they cannot support

options.text: Discard the failing ticket, since a customer who could not check out is not a real case of the change.
options.misconception: discards a case because its outcome was a failure

questions.explanation: The failing ticket supports a close account of what went wrong, and the succeeding one shows the outcome turned on the address format too. Two accounts give no rate, and failure cases are often the most informative.
questions.hint: Ask what each ticket shows about the address format.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: Select the conclusion a trace best supports
questions.stem: A trace shows: a queue fills, workers become saturated, requests start failing, and an alert fires. Which conclusion is best supported by this trace?

options.text: The queue filling caused the failures, because each step in the trace follows logically from the one before it.
options.misconception: treats logical succession in a trace as a demonstrated link

options.text: The alert firing caused the failures, because the alert is the event the team noticed and acted on.
options.misconception: picks the most visible event in a trace as the cause of the rest

options.text: The failures followed the saturation in the recorded order, while the link between filling and saturation remains untested.
The trace shows the whole system failed at once, because the four events appear within the same trace.
options.misconception: reads a group of recorded events as a single simultaneous failure

questions.explanation: The trace fixes the order, so the failures did follow the saturation. It does not show that filling the queue produced the saturation, since nothing in the trace varies one condition at a time.
questions.hint: Ask which link in the trace has actually been tested.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unobserved step inside a traced chain
questions.learningObjective: Handle an unrecorded step inside a chain
questions.stem: A chain runs from a licence change to a compliance report that no longer matches reality. The step that would connect them is a manual correction nobody logged. What is the right response?

options.text: Report the chain as it stands, since each of the two recorded events is itself well documented.
options.misconception: treats well documented ends as if they licensed the whole chain

options.text: Report only the licence change, since the report is too vague to be worth including.
options.misconception: drops one event because the other is described in general terms

options.text: Include the manual correction with a note that the team believes it happened, since the order is not in doubt.
options.misconception: presents an unrecorded event as part of the documented record

options.text: Mark the middle step as inferred, and either find its record or state the gap in the account.

questions.explanation: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and a manual correction nobody logged cannot be presented as part of the record. Marking it as inferred and stating the gap keeps the account honest.
questions.hint: Decide how to handle the step that no record supports.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rival explanation and the test that separates them
questions.learningObjective: Recognise decisive evidence against two rival explanations
questions.stem: Two explanations compete for a missing file: the disk was full, and a scheduled cleanup removed it early. What would count as a decisive piece of evidence?

options.text: A record showing the disk had free space while the cleanup job was also disabled, which rules out both explanations.
A record showing the disk was full, which by itself settles the question in favour of the first explanation.
options.misconception: accepts support for one explanation as though it excluded the other

options.text: A report that other teams have seen the same file go missing, which shows the file is genuinely important.
options.misconception: judges the question by the importance of the affected file

options.text: A note from the engineer who owns the job, saying the cleanup timing was changed last month.
options.misconception: relies on recollection rather than a record of the two conditions

questions.explanation: Decisive evidence changes what is possible under each explanation, and the record described removes the conditions each one needed. Showing the disk was full supports one without excluding the other.
questions.hint: Ask what the evidence rules out, not what it supports.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: Explain when a deviant case is the more valuable choice
questions.stem: A team must choose one ticket to represent the rest of a batch about failed notifications. Explain what they should look at and why a deviant case may be the better choice.

answer.exemplar: First the team must establish the pattern the batch actually shares, since the batch was collected around notification failures and its tickets may differ in sender, device, time of day and message length, and any of these could be producing the failures. Once the pattern is clear, a ticket that departs from it is often the more valuable choice, because it is the case where the existing account has to be extended, and the extension is what reveals whether the account was ever right. Choosing the most dramatic ticket instead would only produce a vivid case with no evidential value.

questions.explanation: First establish the pattern the batch shares, since several features could produce the failures. A deviant case is often better, because it is where the account must be extended.
questions.hint: Check the shared pattern before choosing which case to lead with.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: Spot a condition confounded with the one under study

stimulus.body: A researcher pairs a ticket from a customer on a legacy export format with a ticket from a customer on the current format. Both report the same export failure, and the two customers use the same account manager, the same week and the same file size. The legacy customer is the only one of the two who had a third-party tool reading the exported file.

questions.stem: Given this thread, what is the strongest reading of the pair?

options.text: The pair is well matched on every feature that matters, so the format alone explains the failure.
options.misconception: assumes the listed matches cover every relevant condition

options.text: The pair is matched on the visible features but not on the third-party tool, so the format is confounded with another difference.
The pair should be discarded, because the third-party tool makes the two customers unlike in every respect.
options.misconception: discards a pair because one unmatched feature exists

options.text: The pair supports a general claim about export formats, because both customers reported the same failure.
options.misconception: extends a two-case pair into a general claim about formats

questions.explanation: Matching on account manager, week and file size leaves the third-party tool free to vary with the format, so the pair cannot separate the two. The failure is consistent with either difference.
questions.hint: Look for what varies alongside the condition of interest.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: Read a pair whose conditions move together without guessing a cause
questions.stem: A pair of tickets reports the same failure but differs on device age, app version and network type. Which claim does the pair best support?

options.text: That old devices fail more often, since the failure recurred in the ticket describing an old device.
options.misconception: picks the case that fits the expected story as the demonstration

options.text: That the failure is caused by network type, since network differences are common in the field.
options.misconception: selects the cause that is most common in the field

options.text: That both cases failed in the same way, while the cause remains unidentified because three conditions moved together.
That the app version is the one factor behind the failures, because versions change more often than hardware.
options.misconception: selects the cause that changes most often in practice

questions.explanation: The pair supports a shared description of the failure, not its cause, since three conditions moved together and each could account for it. Choosing among them by preference would be a guess.
questions.hint: Check whether the cause is identified or still open.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: Publish a claim that stays inside the comparison behind it
questions.stem: A team has matched two tickets and wants to publish the result in a release note. What should the team do before writing the claim?

options.text: Publish a general claim, because a release note reaches readers who were not part of the comparison.
options.misconception: widens the claim because the note reaches a wider audience

options.text: Check the effect size and drop the comparison if it is small, since small effects never support claims.
options.misconception: treats effect size as the condition for making any claim at all

options.text: Add the tickets to the release note as evidence, since readers cannot check the matching themselves.
options.misconception: assumes readers cannot check the match, so no limit is needed

options.text: Write the claim for the cases compared, name the conditions held constant, and drop the general version.

questions.explanation: The claim should match the comparison: the cases compared, with the conditions held constant named. A wider audience is a reason to state the limit clearly, and effect size does not change what was held steady.
questions.hint: Write the claim to match the comparison exactly.
